Yes, I am urgently selling a pony.
I sure am selling it, I am waiting for you.
Ainura, quickly clean everything up here.
I came to work in Moscow.
And now I am cleaning up after a horse.

words.gloss: to remove, to take away; to tidy up

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Look for him upstairs quickly!
Let us vote fairly and quickly!
Quickly restore order in the hotel!

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'вести'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to establish, bring', paired with 'наводить'.

examples.trans: I will establish iron order here.

examples.text: Дежурный офицер навёл идеальный порядок в части.
examples.trans: The duty officer established ideal order in the unit.

examples.text: Да, я наведу здесь железный порядок.
examples.trans: Yes, I will establish iron order here.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Thank goodness, this is treatable now.
An urgent operation in Germany is needed.
Actually, it is a big problem.

meanings.note: Agent/instrument noun formed with the productive Slavic suffix '-тель' ('-er'). Common masculine noun meaning 'hotel' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: But after all, he is my father.
I built a hotel in Saint Petersburg.

examples.text: Я просто хотел спросить про отца.
examples.trans: I just wanted to ask about your father.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'рядок'). Formed with a diminutive/expressive Slavic suffix adding warmth or small scale. Common masculine noun meaning 'order' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Quickly restore order in the hotel!
Now let's go through everything in order.
Everything is in complete order.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'otherwise', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: We start work right now!
He happens to need horsemeat right now.
Maybe we could have dinner together now?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: His condition is stable but serious.
Thank goodness, this is treatable now.
An urgent operation in Germany is needed.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Are you the boss in here now, or what?
You are a completely irresponsible cook.

examples.text: Михаил Джекович коня в карты выиграл.
examples.trans: Mikhail Jekovich won a horse at cards.

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'сюда').

examples.trans: Go on out of here, call the next person in.
Otherwise I will throw you out of here.
That is it, get out of here quickly!

meanings.note: Prefix 'вы-' ('out of') marks outward movement or thorough completion (stem 'швырнуть'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'I will throw out'.

related.gloss: to I will throw out (prefixed perfective)
not to I will throw out (negated infinitive)

examples.trans: Otherwise I will throw you out of here.

examples.text: Надо всё сделать и вышвырнуть вовремя.
examples.trans: We need to do everything and I will throw out on time.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: His condition is stable but serious.
Thank goodness, this is treatable now.
An urgent operation in Germany is needed.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you (polite/plural)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Lyova has a bad leg sprain.
He is sidelined for about a week.
Let us hold fair elections here.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian cardinal or ordinal numeral meaning 'two', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I cannot leave him in the courtyard.
This is Denis, my first cousin.
Let us sum up the results of our fair contest.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лушать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to listen', paired with 'послушать'.

examples.trans: Listen, well done, you know how to bargain well.
And you two listen to me.
Listen, Samson.

meanings.note: Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'деля'). Common feminine noun meaning 'week' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: He is sidelined for about a week.
For a week we will manage somehow by ourselves.
We worked three weeks without the chef.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'work', paired with 'поработать'.

examples.trans: We worked three weeks without the chef.
Here, take this and work!
Thank you, guys, let us work now.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'овсем').

examples.trans: You are a completely irresponsible cook.
Why, it is completely fresh, for sure.

examples.text: Потому что она совсем не свежая.
examples.trans: Because it is not fresh at all.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'without', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Just no panic at all for now.
We worked three weeks without the chef.
You are a completely irresponsible cook.

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'рплата'). Common feminine noun meaning 'paychecks' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I am docking all of you a day's salary.
You will work a week with no salary at all.
He lives on his salary.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: His condition is stable but serious.
Thank goodness, this is treatable now.
An urgent operation in Germany is needed.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian cardinal or ordinal numeral meaning 'two', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Fine, but take two crates.
We have two kinds of ballots.

examples.text: Операция будет в два раза дороже.
examples.trans: The operation will be twice as expensive.

meanings.note: Prefix 'вы-' ('out of') marks outward movement or thorough completion (stem 'ходной'). Common masculine noun meaning 'weekend' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: And two weeks without days off.
It's a day off, after all.

examples.text: Что ты делаешь в эти выходные?
examples.trans: What are you doing this weekend?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'everything', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: That is it, candidate registration is already closed.
I understand everything perfectly.

examples.text: А потом мы обо всём поговорим.
examples.trans: And later we will talk about everything.

meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to go (set off)', paired with 'идти'.

examples.trans: We have already caught her!
May I go?
Let's go home.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'over there', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: That is it, get out of here quickly!
You did not even call your beloved aunt!
Strange, why did he not call?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'no', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I do not have that kind of money.
No, it did not work out again today.
No, one cannot do that at all.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this, it (is)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: By estimates this costs a lot.
Actually, it is a big problem.
Wait, this is not a horse.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I do not have that kind of money.
Money is not a problem, right, Mom?
There is no need to sell anything right now.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'yes', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Money is not a problem, right, Mom?
I can sell my apartment.
There is no need to sell anything right now.

meanings.en: urgently, right away; predicative: it is urgent
meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'рочно'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: An urgent operation in Germany is needed.
I need to step out urgently for a minute.
In the morning I ate expired yogurt.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'давать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to sell'.

examples.trans: There is no need to sell anything right now.
How much are you selling them for?

examples.text: Конечно надо! Почём ты их продаёшь?
examples.trans: Of course I do! How much are you selling them for?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'pony' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: On the other hand, he is a very thoroughbred pony.
A Japanese delegation has checked in with us.
The Japanese refused to eat this fish.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'else/more', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I will also give you a good discount.
And tomorrow we will buy even more fish.
And he also loves carrots.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'how', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: For a week we will manage somehow by ourselves.
It has a rather exhausted look.
What a handsome fellow, such a plump horse.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'am waiting for', paired with 'подождать'.

examples.trans: Am I supposed to sit and wait?
Don't wait for me.
I'm waiting for you.

meanings.en: to remove, to take away, to cut out
meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'брать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'take away, remove', paired with 'убирать'.

examples.text: Ты можешь убрать весь этот шум?
examples.trans: Can you cut out all this noise?
Take the phone off the table.

examples.text: Так, ты можешь убрать весь этот шум? Нам нужен только Аникеев.
examples.trans: Right, can you cut out all this noise? We only need Anikeev.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'here', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Let us hold fair elections here.
We are looking for money everywhere right now.
Stand here and guard the horse.

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'ехать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'came, arrived (she)', paired with 'приезжать'.

examples.trans: Did the horse arrive to pay off an old debt?
I came to work in Moscow.
You came to Moscow and kept quiet.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'now', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Are you the boss in here now, or what?
Captain, take this, this is for you now.
Great, now you have voted fairly.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'бирать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to clean up, to tidy', paired with 'убрать'.

examples.trans: And now I am cleaning up after a horse.
I'm cleaning the flat.
Who cleans the kitchen?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Я большой кредит под залог взяла.
examples.trans: I took out a big loan against collateral.
Viktor Petrovich will definitely recover soon.
On the other hand, he is a very thoroughbred pony.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'horse; knight (in chess)' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: That is it, candidate registration is already closed.

examples.text: Михаил Джекович коня в карты выиграл.
examples.trans: Mikhail Jekovich won a horse at cards.
Did the horse arrive to pay off an old debt?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ейчас').

examples.trans: Thank goodness, this is treatable now.
There is no need to sell anything right now.
Quiet, there is no need to argue now.
